title: Parallel (1+e)-Approximate Multi-Commodity Min-Cost Flow in Almost Optimal Depth and Work
authors: Bernhard Haeupler (University of Sofia "St. Kliment Ohridski" and ETH Zürich), Yonggang Jiang (MPI-INF and Saarland University), Yaowei Long (University of Michigan), Thatchaphol Saranurak (University of Michigan), Shengzhe Wang (ETH Zürich)
abstract: We present a parallel algorithm for computing $(1+\epsilon)$-approximate min-cost flow on an undirected graph with $m$ edges, where capacities and costs are assigned to both edges and vertices. Our algorithm achieves $\hat{O}(m)$ work and $\hat{O}(1)$ depth when $\epsilon > 1/polylog(m)$, making both the work and depth almost optimal, up to a subpolynomial factor. Previous algorithms with $\hat{O}(m)$ work required $\Omega(m)$ depth, even for special cases of min-cost flow with only edge capacities or max flow with vertex capacities. Our result generalizes prior almost-optimal parallel $(1+\epsilon)$-approximation algorithms for these special cases, including shortest paths [Li, STOC'20] [Andoni, Stein, Zhong, STOC'20] [Rozhen, Grunau, Haeupler, Zuzic, Li, STOC'22] and max flow with only edge capacities [Li, Nanongkai, Panigrahi, Saranurak, SODA'23] [Agarwal, Khanna, Li, Patil, Wang, White, Zhong, SODA'24]. Our key technical contribution is the first construction of length-constrained flow shortcuts with $(1+\epsilon)$ length slack, $\hat{O}(1)$ congestion slack, and $\hat{O}(1)$ step bound. This provides a strict generalization of the influential concept of $(\hat{O}(1),\epsilon)$-hopsets [Cohen, JACM'00], allowing for additional control over congestion. Previous length-constrained flow shortcuts [Haeupler, Hershkowitz, Li, Roeyskoe, Saranurak, STOC'24] incur a large constant in the length slack, which would lead to a large approximation factor. To enable our flow algorithms to work under vertex capacities, we also develop a close-to-linear time algorithm for computing length-constrained vertex expander decomposition. Building on Cohen's idea of path-count flows [Cohen, SICOMP'95], we further extend our algorithm to solve $(1+\epsilon)$-approximate k-commodity min-cost flow problems with almost-optimal $\hat{O}(mk)$ work and $\hat{O}(1)$ depth, independent of the number of commodities k.

Abstract—We present a parallel algorithm for computing (1 +
ϵ)-approximate min-cost flow on an undirected graph with m
edges, where capacities and costs are assigned to both edges and
vertices. Our algorithm achieves Ô(m) work and Ô(1) depth
when ϵ > 1/polylog(m), making both the work and depth almost
optimal, up to a subpolynomial factor.
Previous algorithms with Ô(m) work required Ω(m) depth,
even for special cases of min-cost flow with only edge capacities
or max flow with vertex capacities. Our result generalizes prior
almost-optimal parallel (1 + ϵ)-approximation algorithms for
these special cases, including shortest paths [1]–[3] and max flow
with only edge capacities [4], [5].
Our key technical contribution is the first construction of
length-constrained flow shortcuts with (1 + ϵ) length slack, Ô(1)
congestion slack, and Ô(1) step bound. This provides a strict
generalization of the influential concept of (Ô(1), ϵ)-hopsets [6],
allowing for additional control over congestion. Previous lengthconstrained flow shortcuts [7] incur a large constant in the
length slack, which would lead to a large approximation factor.
To enable our flow algorithms to work under vertex capacities,
we also develop a close-to-linear time algorithm for computing
length-constrained vertex expander decomposition.
Building on Cohen’s idea of path-count flows [8], we further
extend our algorithm to solve (1 + ϵ)-approximate k-commodity
min-cost flow problems with almost-optimal Ô(mk) work and
Ô(1) depth, independent of the number of commodities k.
Index Terms—graph algorithms, parallel algorithms, maximum flows, min-cost flows, multi-commodity flows.

A. Our Results
We answer the above open question affirmatively. In particular, we present the first parallel (1 + ϵ)-approximate min-cost
flow algorithm with almost-linear work and subpolynomial
depth for undirected graphs with vertex capacities and costs,
which solves problems 1 and 2 simultaneously.
Formally, consider an n-vertex m-edge graph G = (V, E)
with non-negative polynomially-bounded integral capacities
and costs on both edges and vertices. Let B be a given
number representing the cost budget and s, t ∈ V be two given
vertices. The (1 + ϵ)-approximate min-cost flow problem asks
for a (1 + ϵ)-approximate maximum flow among all flows that
have total cost at most B and respect the capacity on each
edge and vertex. Our result is formally stated in Theorem 1.
Theorem 1. Given a graph G, cost budget B, two vertices
s, t ∈ V , and a precision parameter 1/polylog(n) < ϵ <
1, there exists a parallel (1 + ϵ)-approximate min-cost flow
algorithm with Ô(m) work and Ô(1) depth.

B. Our Techniques
We now highlight our technical components that may be
of independent interest. An overview of how everything fits
together will be given in Section II.
Length-Constrained Flow Shortcuts with (1 + ϵ) Length
Slack. The notion of length-constrained flow shortcuts3 (LCflow shortcuts) are introduced recently by [7], which is a
new kind of graph augmentation capturing both length and
congestion information. Roughly speaking, an LC-flow shortcut augments a graph with additional edges and vertices,
enabling all multi-commodity flow demands to be routed with
approximately the same length and congestion as before, but
only along flow paths each of which has a small number
(called step) of edges.
[7] showed the existence of an LC-flow shortcut of size
O(n1+O(ϵ) ) with length slack O(1/ϵ3 ), congestion slack nO(ϵ)
and O(1/ϵ) step4 , but for undirected graphs with only edge
lengths and capacities. They also presented shortcuts that can
be constructed in parallel and fast but with worse quality such
as 2poly(1/ϵ) length slack. For undirected graphs with vertex
lengths and capacities, very recently, [43] showed that there
exists an LC-flow shortcut of size O(n1+O(ϵ) ) with length
slack O(1/ϵ3 ), congestion slack nO(ϵ) and step 2O(1/ϵ) , but
without an efficient construction.
The approaches behind both the aforementioned LC-flow
shortcuts are based on tools related to length-constrained
(vertex) expanders [43]–[45]. However, these approaches fail
to go beyond the inherent large length slack of these tools,
and therefore do not result in LC-flow shortcuts with 1 + ϵ
length slack.
We give the first LC-flow shortcut with 1 + ϵ length slack.
Precisely, our LC-flow shortcut works for undirected graphs
with vertex lengths and capacities, and it has size Ô(n),
length slack 1 + ϵ, congestion slack Ô(1) and step Ô(1) for
any 1/polylog(n) < ϵ < 1. Furthermore, our shortcut can
be constructed in Ô(m) work and Ô(1) depth. We refer to
Theorem 5.2 in the full version for a detailed statement of our
result (or Theorem 3 in the overview for an informal version).
Our new LC-flow shortcut, thus, improves upon previous
length slack from a large constant to (1 + ϵ), at an expense of
increasing the step from a large constant to Ô(1). However,
the step will only affect the work and depth of the final algorithms, not the approximation. The construction of our LCflow shortcuts can be viewed as a generalization of Cohen’s
hopset construction [6] which provides shortcuts with (1 + ϵ)
length slack but no guarantee on congestion slack.

Length-Constrained Multi-Commodity Maxflows in Low
Depths. Our last intermediate result which may be of independent interest is a (1+ϵ)-approximate length-constrained multicommodity maxflow algorithm with Õ(mk)·poly(h, ϵ−1 ) work
and Õ(1) · poly(h, ϵ−1 ) depth, for k commodities and a given
h representing the length constraint. We refer to Section 6 in
the full version for the formal definition and Theorem 6.1 in
the full version for the formal result statement.
Previously, [47] studied this problem in the singlecommodity setting, and showed a single-commodity version
with Õ(m) · poly(h, ϵ−1 ) work and Õ(1) · poly(h, ϵ−1 ). They
also generalized their result to the multi-commodity setting in
an (almost) black-box way, but with an additional k factor in
depth compared to ours.
Our approach towards improvement (i.e. the depth is now
independent from k) is a white-box generalization of [47]
combining Cohen’s idea of path-count flows [8].

Lastly, we make some comments on making the above shortcut

existence of such decompositions was shown in a recent work

In this part, given a demand D, we want to compute a flow
F routing D in G with low congestion (say Õ(1) or Ô(1)),
such that the total length (i.e. cost) of F is within a 1 + O(ϵ)
multiplicative factor from the min-total-length t-step feasible
flow F ∗ routing D.
This problem can be reduced to the (approximate) lengthconstrained maximum flow problem, which has been studied
by [47] but mainly in the single-commodity setting. Intuitively,
the reduction is a simple greedy strategy. Since congestion
Õ(1) is allowed, we can consider length parameter h = (1 +
ϵ)i in an increasing order of i. For each such h, we try to
route as much demand as possible using a feasible h-length.
Concretely, we partially route D via a feasible (1 + ϵ)h-length
flow Fh with value (approximately) at least the maximum tstep h-length feasible flow Fh∗ partially routing D. Add this Fh
into F , subtract from D the demand that has been routed, and
then go to the next h. A small issue is that the LC-max flow
subroutine will have work and depth depending on poly(h) (as
we will see soon), so we cannot compute Fh directly when h
is large. However, since we only need value(Fh ) comparable
to the value of the t-step h-length Fh∗ , we actually allow ϵh/t
additive errors on the edge lengths. Hence we can just scale
down the edge length by ϵh/t (then round up to integers) and
compute a (t/ϵ + t)-length maxflow instead.

III. C ONCLUSIONS AND O PEN P ROBLEMS
In this work, we present a parallel (1+ϵ)-approximate multicommodity min-cost flow algorithm with almost optimal work
and depth, which applies to undirected graphs with capacities
and costs on both edges and vertices. Our key technical
contribution is devising an LC-flow shortcut with 1 + ϵ length
slack, Ô(1) congestion slack, and Ô(1) step, which has size
Ô(n) and can be computed in Ô(m) work and Ô(1) depth.
Our work also leaves several interesting open problems.

Distributed Min-cost Flows. Parallel and distributed algorithms are closely related, and there have been many technical
transfers between the two settings. For example, [3] studies
the (1 + ϵ)-approximate shortest path problem in parallel and
distributed settings simultaneously.
As we give the almost-optimal parallel algorithm for (1+ϵ)approximate min-cost flow problem, a natural next step is to
solve it almost-optimally in the distributed setting. We note
that there has been distributed (1 + ϵ)-approximate (singlecommodity) maxflow algorithms with almost-optimal round
complexity in the CONGEST model [53]. However, analogous results for the min-cost flow problem remain unclear,
though there have been some efforts on distributed exact mincost flow in directed graphs [54], [55].

Polylogarithmic Depth. A natural and important open problem is to further reduce the depth from subpolynomial to polylogarithmic while retaining almost-optimal work or improving
toward nearly-optimal work, even in the single-commodity setting. As we discussed in Section I, (1+ϵ)-approximate parallel
algorithms with polylogarithmic depth and nearly-linear work
are known for shortest paths [1]–[3] and (edge-capacitated)
maxflows [5]. However, it remains unclear whether similar
results (particularly polylogarithmic depth) can be achieved
for the (edge-capacitated) min-cost flow problem or vertexcapacitated maxflow problem.
Open Problem 1. Are there parallel (1 + ϵ)-approximate
algorithms for either (edge-capacitated) min-cost flows or
vertex-capacitated maximum flows, with nearly-linear work
and polylogarithmic depth?

Open Problem 2. Is there distributed (1 + ϵ)-approximate
min-cost flow algorithm with almost-optimal round complexity
in the CONGEST model?
We note that our approach may potentially transfer to the
distributed setting, since the main building blocks, including
length-constrained expander decompositions, sparse neighborhood cover, and approximate length-constrained maxflows, all
admit efficient distributed algorithms.
